reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant condition of lifelong mild hypercalcaemia that is usually asymptomatic and benign
Most commonly caused by heterozygous inactivating mutations in the calcium-sensing receptor gene CASR
The defining biochemical feature is hypercalcaemia with inappropriately low urinary calcium excretion
Parathyroid hormone is typically normal or only mildly elevated, mimicking mild primary hyperparathyroidism
A low urinary calcium to creatinine clearance ratio is the key discriminator from primary hyperparathyroidism
The condition does not respond to and should not be treated with parathyroidectomy
Homozygous or biallelic mutations cause severe neonatal hyperparathyroidism, a life-threatening contrast to the mild heterozygous form
reference.pathophysiology: The calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid and renal tubular cells detects extracellular calcium and regulates PTH secretion and renal calcium handling. Inactivating CASR mutations blunt this sensing, so a higher calcium concentration is required to suppress PTH and the kidney reabsorbs calcium avidly. The set point for calcium is effectively reset upward, producing stable mild hypercalcaemia with characteristically reduced urinary calcium. Because the abnormality is intrinsic to calcium sensing rather than to parathyroid mass, removing parathyroid tissue does not correct the hypercalcaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Vitamin D or vitamin A toxicity
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium, phosphate and intact parathyroid hormone
Twenty-four-hour urinary calcium with calculation of the calcium to creatinine clearance ratio
Serum magnesium, which is often at the upper end or mildly elevated
Molecular genetic testing of CASR and related genes
Family biochemical screening to demonstrate autosomal dominant hypercalcaemia
redFlags: Severe neonatal hypercalcaemia suggesting biallelic disease and requiring emergency management
Marked hypercalcaemic symptoms that are atypical for the usually benign heterozygous form
Coexisting features that raise concern for primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy
Renal complications such as stones or nephrocalcinosis prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The heterozygous form is benign with an excellent prognosis, requiring recognition and reassurance rather than intervention, whereas the neonatal severe form is a medical emergency with a very different outlook.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as primary hyperparathyroidism and performing an unnecessary parathyroidectomy
Failing to measure urinary calcium, missing the discriminating hypocalciuria
Overlooking the autosomal dominant family history of asymptomatic hypercalcaemia
Not recognising that biallelic mutations cause severe neonatal disease
management: Recognise the disorder to avoid inappropriate parathyroidectomy, since removing parathyroid tissue does not correct the reset calcium set-point
Reassure and observe, as the benign heterozygous form needs no specific drug therapy
Confirm with a low urinary calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio to differentiate it from primary hyperparathyroidism
Maintain hydration and avoid thiazide diuretics, lithium and vitamin D or calcium excess that worsen the hypercalcaemia
Reserve a calcimimetic (cinacalcet) for the rare symptomatic patient
Undertake autosomal dominant family biochemical screening and genetic counselling for CASR variants
Treat neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism in homozygous infants as an emergency, potentially requiring urgent parathyroidectomy
